title: Contagion Live: Addressing the Hepatitis D Testing Gap Through Reflex Screening
summary: Charles M. Walworth, M.D., associate vice president of medical affairs and education and co-discipline director for molecular infectious diseases at Labcorp, recently joined the Contagion Live podcast, From Pathogen to Infectious Disease Diagnosis, to discuss the longstanding challenge of underdiagnosed hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection and the role of reflex testing in expanding detection.
body_markdown:
Charles M. Walworth, M.D., associate vice president of medical affairs and education and co-discipline director for molecular infectious diseases at Labcorp, recently joined the *Contagion Live* podcast, *From Pathogen to Infectious Disease Diagnosis* , to discuss the longstanding challenge of underdiagnosed hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection and the role of reflex testing in expanding detection.


**Key takeaway:** Labcorp has introduced a physician-ordered reflex testing option that automatically screens for hepatitis D when hepatitis B is detected, helping close a significant gap in diagnosis.


**Why it matters:** Hepatitis D is considered the most severe form of viral hepatitis and is associated with accelerated liver disease progression, including cirrhosis and liver failure. Despite clinical guidelines recommending screening for patients with hepatitis B, fewer than 20% of eligible patients in the U.S. are estimated to be tested for HDV.


During the discussion, Walworth reflected on patients with hepatitis B whose disease progressed more rapidly than expected despite appropriate risk reduction and clinical management, underscoring the historical lack of accessible hepatitis D testing and the likelihood that some cases of co-infection went undiagnosed.


The need for improved detection has taken on greater urgency following the FDA approval of bulevirtide-gmod (Hepcludex) in May 2026, the first treatment specifically indicated for hepatitis D. In response, Labcorp launched a reflex testing protocol that allows clinicians to automatically perform hepatitis D testing on the same specimen when hepatitis B is detected, eliminating the need for an additional patient visit or blood draw.


The strategy builds on the success of reflex testing in hepatitis C, where streamlined screening and diagnostic pathways have helped identify more patients earlier in the course of disease. Labcorp researchers recently analyzed more than 38 million hepatitis C specimens collected between 2018 and 2024, with findings published in[Clinical Infectious Diseases](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article-abstract/82/6/988/8643933?login=false) . The same approach is now being applied to support earlier identification and treatment of hepatitis D.


**Listen to the full podcast on**[Contagion Live.](https://www.contagionlive.com/view/from-pathogen-to-infectious-disease-diagnosis-reflex-testing-targets-hepatitis-d-gap)
